questions.stem: Project K, with an NPV of $2,000k, is in a best plan worth $30,000k. Forced out and re-solved, the best plan is worth $29,850k. What is K worth to the plan?

options.text: $2,000k, since dropping K takes exactly its own NPV out of the plan
options.says: The re-solve spends K's money on other projects, so the plan loses far less than K's NPV, as P032 lost $112k against $3,678k.

options.text: $29,850k, since that is the value the plan keeps once K is gone
options.says: That is the forced plan's value; K's worth is the difference between the two optima.

options.text: $1,850k, since K's NPV less the forced plan's loss is what K adds
options.says: The cost of the decision is the loss itself, z* less the forced optimum, not NPV less loss.

options.text: $150k, since the money K frees is spent on the next best projects
options.says: Right: $30,000k less $29,850k. K's money is reused, so its worth to the plan is far below its own NPV.

origin.section: The Cost of a Decision Is What the Best Plan Loses When You Force the Opposite

questions.stem: A planner forces project W out of a capital plan, and the re-solve ends INFEASIBLE. What should the report's line for W say?

options.text: That removing W breaks a rule, naming the rows in conflict, with no cost
options.says: Right: an infeasible forcing has no optimum to compare, so the answer is the rule, such as must_P017 against out_P017.

options.text: That W costs the whole plan's NPV, since no plan at all remains without W
options.says: No plan means no forced optimum, so there is no difference to report; the cost is undefined, not the whole NPV.

options.text: That W costs nothing, since the re-solve returned no plan to compare with
options.says: A zero cost means another optimal plan obeys the forcing; here no plan obeys it at all.

options.text: That W is worth its own NPV, since the solver found no project to replace it
options.says: INFEASIBLE says no plan keeps the rules with W out, not that nothing could replace W.

origin.section: A Forcing the Rules Cannot Satisfy Is Answered by a Rule, Not a Price

questions.stem: Forcing project N into a plan worth $40,000k costs $6k, and three other forcings land on that very same plan. How should the report read N's decision?

options.text: The decision marks N as weak, since the solver left it out
options.says: A plan with N is within $6k of the best; the solver had to pick one of two nearly equal plans.

options.text: The decision shows an unreliable solver, since rivals this close are rare
options.says: Close runner-up plans are normal; GridCap small has one $8k below its proven optimum.

options.text: The decision is a near tie, and overriding it is cheap
options.says: Right: a plan with N is almost as good; the decision is cheap to override and could flip with small input changes.

options.text: The decision points to a model error, since its cost is under 1%
options.says: A small cost is a finding about near ties, not evidence of a modeling error.

origin.section: Report Every Project, and Read Small Costs as Near Ties
